lectures.title: Type 1 vs Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
lectures.framing: Both types are diagnosed by the same glucose thresholds — what separates them is the mechanism producing the hyperglycemia: absolute autoimmune insulin deficiency vs. a spectrum of insulin resistance and relative deficiency.
lectures.keypoints: the alpha cells are spared in T1DM — the lesion is beta-cell specific. Autoantibody count, not presence, is what carries risk (1 = background risk, 3 = 40% in five years). Glutamic acid decarboxylase is the specific marker. Monozygotic concordance is higher in T2DM (90%) than T1DM (50%) — the counterintuitive fact worth remembering. And the octet explains why T2DM needs combination therapy: each drug class corrects a different defect.

lectures.name: Diagnosis and Management of Type 1 Diabetes
lectures.title: Approach to New-Onset Type 1 Diabetes
lectures.framing: The whole diagnosis turns on one question: are symptoms present? If yes, a single abnormal glucose is sufficient — do not delay treatment for a confirmatory test.
lectures.keypoints: symptoms present → one abnormal glucose diagnoses diabetes; no symptoms → two are needed. The Diabetes Control and Complications Trial logic underlies everything here — intensive insulin therapy ↓ A1c and ↓ long-term microvascular complications but ↑ hypoglycemia, a trade-off now partly offset by pumps and continuous glucose monitors. Glucose gel works through buccal mucosa, so it can be given when swallowing is unsafe.

blocks.html: Workup skeleton

• History — the three classic early symptoms nearly every patient has: polyuria (including nocturia / new bed-wetting), excessive thirst, weight loss despite unchanged or ↑ appetite. Then screen for late/severe features: vomiting, abdominal pain, dehydration, hyperventilation, fatigue, ↓ level of consciousness.
  • Physical exam — hydration status, weight loss, level of consciousness, Kussmaul breathing, acetone breath.
  • Investigations — random plasma glucose ≥ 11.1, urine dipstick for glucose and ketones, serum C-peptide (is she making any insulin?), arterial blood gas if DKA suspected. ⚠ Fasting plasma glucose (FPG) and glycated hemoglobin (A1c) are usually unnecessary here — the diagnosis is already clear.
  • Treatment — insulin + structured education; treat DKA emergently if present.
  • Follow-up — annual urinalysis for albuminuria (diabetic nephropathy screening).

lectures.name: Pharmacology of Insulin
lectures.title: Insulin Preparations
lectures.framing: Choose a preparation based on what the insulin is covering — a meal (bolus) or the fasting state (basal). Onset and duration are set by one thing: how fast monomers dissociate from the hexamer, since insulin binds its receptor only as a monomer. Anything that stabilizes the hexamer (zinc, protamine, self-aggregation, albumin binding) → slower onset, longer duration.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Analogues are NOT more effective at lowering glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) than human insulin — they are safer and more convenient (faster onset, better postprandial match, lower variability, less nocturnal hypoglycemia). Only regular insulin can be given intravenously. Basal insulins must never be used in pumps, and most basal insulins must not be mixed with another insulin before injection. Insulin does not interfere with the absorption or metabolism of other drugs — but drugs that alter glucose metabolism (e.g. steroids ↑ hepatic glucose production) change how well it works. Exogenous insulin is imperfect because physiological secretion is glucose-dependent, and that fine-tuning is lost.

lectures.name: Clinically Useful Endocrine Principles
lectures.title: Approach to a Suspected Endocrine Problem
lectures.framing: Every endocrine problem sorts into structural (a mass) or functional (too much or too little hormone) — and both can be present at once. The sorting question determines the entire workup.
lectures.keypoints: the suppression/stimulation pairing is the single most testable idea here — excess is tested by trying to turn it off, deficiency by trying to turn it on. primary adrenal insufficiency loses both cortisol AND aldosterone, which is what separates it from central causes. A benign mass can still be clinically important through pure mass effect. And always ask whether an exogenous hormone explains the picture before working up the gland.

blocks.lead: Four questions to ask of any functional problem: What does the hormone do? · What feedback loops could be affected? · Is the problem in the gland itself (primary) or somewhere else (secondary / tertiary / central)? · Can this be explained by an exogenous source of hormone?

lectures.name: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus - Diagnosis & Epidemiology
lectures.title: Diagnosing Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) and the Grey Zone
lectures.framing: Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) and T2DM share identical diagnostic thresholds — so the diagnostic work is (1) crossing the threshold, (2) deciding how many measurements you need, and (3) working out which type you are looking at.
lectures.keypoints: symptomatic → one measurement; asymptomatic → two. Do not diagnose during acute illness (myocardial infarction, sepsis, steroids) — suspect, then confirm on recovery. C-peptide and anti-GAD move in opposite directions between the two types: low C-peptide + high anti-GAD = T1DM. >90% of all diabetes is Type 2; 589 million adults live with diabetes worldwide (~1 in 9), ~43% of them undiagnosed, and ~30% of Canadians have diabetes or prediabetes. Finally — a T2DM diagnosis is not necessarily permanent: weight loss, activity and diet can return glucose below the diabetic range, though it can recur, so keep checking a few times a year.

lectures.framing: The acute emergencies separate on one variable: is there enough insulin to suppress lipolysis? Enough → no ketones → hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS). Not enough → ketogenesis → diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA).
lectures.keypoints: abdominal pain and vomiting = DKA, not HHS. Hours = DKA, days = HHS. T1DM = DKA, older T2DM = HHS. SGLT2 inhibitors can precipitate DKA — and appear again in the sick-day rules as a drug to stop. Potassium falls with treatment, not before it. Proprioception goes early in peripheral neuropathy, and feet are affected before hands because of nerve length.

lectures.framing: Obesity is a complex, progressive, relapsing chronic disease — abnormal or excessive body fat that impairs health. BMI alone does not predict adiposity-related complications; stage the impact, not just the number.
lectures.keypoints: tirzepatide (dual GLP-1/glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide) beats semaglutide beats naltrexone-bupropion for weight loss. The most serious post-bariatric deficiency is thiamine — give it before any glucose or you precipitate Wernicke's encephalopathy. The BMI cut-off drops to 25 for South and East Asian patients. The pharmacotherapy stopping rule is 5% at 12 weeks. Gastric banding is explicitly not recommended. lectures.name: Pregnancy and Diabetes
lectures.title: Diabetes in Pregnancy
lectures.framing: The single discriminating question is when the hyperglycemia starts. Pre-existing diabetes mellitus (DM) is present during organogenesis (weeks 3–16) → congenital malformations. Gestational diabetes (GDM) appears at 24–28 weeks, after organogenesis → NO congenital malformations, but the same fetal morbidities.
lectures.keypoints: GDM does not cause congenital malformations; pre-existing DM does — because of when the hyperglycemia occurs relative to organogenesis. Insulin needs FALL in trimester 1 and after delivery, and RISE steeply in trimester 3. Glyburide crosses the placenta; insulin does not. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers are contraindicated — use beta-blockers or calcium channel blockers. Retinopathy that worsens in pregnancy usually settles after delivery without permanent damage, but screen pre-conception, during, and within the first postpartum year. Fetal death risk is low (0.6–4.8%) — malformation risk is the greater concern.

lectures.name: Thyroid and Parathyroid Gland Physiology
lectures.title: Thyroid Hormone Synthesis & Calcium Homeostasis
lectures.framing: Two axes, one shape: a gland reacting to a single sensed variable. For the thyroid the sensed variable is circulating triiodothyronine (T3) / thyroxine (T4), read by the hypothalamus and pituitary, and the step the exam turns on is that iodination comes FIRST, then coupling. For the parathyroid the sensed variable is ionized Ca2+, read directly by the chief cell's calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR), and the step it turns on is that ⭐ there is no parathyroid hormone (PTH) receptor in the gut — PTH raises absorbed calcium only indirectly, through calcitriol.
lectures.keypoints: Iodination precedes coupling, and iodide entry is active transport (NIS, then pendrin), never passive diffusion. The goitre of iodine deficiency is not the gland "trying harder" — it is loss of negative feedback → sustained TSH-receptor drive → follicular hypertrophy and hyperplasia, and maternal deficiency is the #1 cause of preventable intellectual disability worldwide. somatostatin inhibits TSH ONLY, not PTH. Calcium is the single discriminator between primary and secondary hyperparathyroidism, and hypocalciuria is what separates FHH from primary. Hashimoto's thyroiditis is anti-TPO, blocking iodination of thyroglobulin, treated with levothyroxine; Graves disease is an activating anti-TSH-receptor antibody with exophthalmos. 99% of body calcium sits in bone as calcium phosphate, and of the 1% in blood 50% is free/ionized — that is the only fraction the CaSR reads and the only fraction that acts.

lectures.title: Approach to Hypothyroidism and Thyrotoxicosis
lectures.framing: The whole evaluation runs on one test in one direction: ⭐ serum thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) to case-find, free hormone only to confirm and grade. TSH works because primary disease, at the gland, is by far the most common kind, and there TSH moves opposite to the hormone. ⚠ That logic inverts in central disease, where pituitary TSH is the broken part and moves with the hormone. Then one further question splits thyrotoxicosis into its causes: is the gland making hormone, or leaking it? — which is what radioactive iodine (RAI) uptake answers.
lectures.keypoints: TSH case-finds, free hormone confirms — and the only reason to break that order is suspected central disease, where TSH and FT4 go together and TSH moves WITH the hormone. RAI uptake answers why, not whether. High uptake = the gland is synthesizing; low uptake = hormone is leaking out of it or coming from a bottle, and low-uptake disease is treated supportively while you watch for the hypothyroid phase. Goiter symmetry is a free discriminator: symmetric points to Graves, asymmetric to nodular disease, and thyroiditis can have no goiter at all. Methimazole is first line for Graves and RAI is first line for nodular disease, because only Graves remits. Levothyroxine's 1-week half-life is why TSH is rechecked at 4 to 6 weeks and not sooner. anti-TPO, anti-thyroglobulin, and ultrasound are the tests to leave alone in straightforward hypothyroidism.

lectures.keypoints: correct for albumin, then always send PTH. Phosphate separates primary from tertiary when calcium cannot — primary drops it because PTH is phosphaturic, tertiary raises it because the failing kidney cannot excrete. PTH-independent hypercalcaemia — over 90% of all hypercalcaemia is hyperparathyroidism or malignancy, so once PTH is suppressed the list is: malignancy (metastases — breast · humoral PTH-related protein — lung, kidney, adult T-cell leukaemia · lymphokines — myeloma) · vitamin D related (exogenous, or granulomatous sarcoid and tuberculosis) · immobilisation on a background of Paget's, thyrotoxicosis or adrenal insufficiency · thiazides · milk-alkali syndrome, acromegaly, phaeochromocytoma, parenteral nutrition.

Hypocalcaemia by phosphate — PTH deficient: Ca↓, phosphate HIGH, PTH low · PTH resistant: Ca↓, phosphate HIGH, PTH high · vitamin D deficient: Ca↓, phosphate LOW, PTH high — and this is the commonest of the three. Minor causes: hypoalbuminaemia, hypomagnesemia, pancreatitis, tumour lysis, rhabdomyolysis, sepsis.

Treating hypercalcaemia — admit if corrected Ca >3 mmol/L. 1. Volume repletion, assume a 4-6 L deficit, normal saline. 2. Forced diuresis, 4-10 L normal saline + furosemide + K⁺, only once well hydrated — LOOP diuretics only, NEVER thiazides, which cause hypercalcaemia. 3. intravenous zoledronate. 4. calcitonin — tachyphylaxis at 24-48 hours, a bridge not a treatment. 5. prednisone 40-60 mg/day where steroids reduce vitamin D activation: myeloma, lymphoma, sarcoidosis, vitamin D toxicity.

Treating hypocalcaemia — only for corrected Ca <1.9 mmol/L with neurological (tetany, seizure, carpopedal spasm) or cardiac (prolonged QT) signs: 1-2 g of 10% calcium gluconate in 50 mL 5% dextrose in water over 15-20 minutes, then 1-3 mg/kg/h, cardiac monitoring, and correct the magnesium.

ECG and symptom split — hypercalcaemia: short QT, Osborn wave, bradycardia, atrioventricular block, weakness and hyporeflexia, nephrolithiasis, pancreatitis, confusion and apathy. Hypocalcaemia: QT PROLONGATION → torsades de pointes, tetany, paraesthesia, brain fog, and chronically cataracts, dry skin, brittle nails. The mechanism of the neuro signs is that low calcium lets sodium channels depolarise more easily.

lectures.title: Thyroid Masses: Clinical Evaluation and Pathology
lectures.framing: Most thyroid nodules are benign (0.1% annual incidence, 10% lifetime probability), so the job is not to find cancer in every nodule but to stratify which nodule earns a biopsy and which biopsy earns an operation. ⭐ Four inputs stack into one decision: clinical risk, biochemistry, imaging, and fine needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB) — together they give risk-adapted management, and none of them is read alone. The order is fixed: thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) first, because a low TSH sends you to a radioactive iodine (RAI) scan before any ultrasound — a HOT nodule is never cancer and stops there, while a COLD nodule comes back to the ultrasound and is scored like any other nodule.
lectures.keypoints: TSH is the first test, because a low TSH diverts you to an RAI scan and a hot nodule is benign; a normal or high TSH goes to ultrasound and TI-RADS. FNA cannot tell a follicular adenoma from a follicular carcinoma (identical nuclei, and only invasion separates them), but it diagnoses papillary carcinoma outright, because in PTC the nuclei are the diagnosis. Graves makes papillary projections without atypia — architecture alone does not mean papillary carcinoma. Amyloid in a thyroid tumour is calcitonin, and means medullary carcinoma, which is RET point mutation while PTC is RET-PTC translocation. Anaplastic carcinoma is what a well-differentiated cancer becomes, and it is the one that will not take up iodine. Needle core biopsy is the wrong instrument for the neck FOR DIAGNOSING A NODULE — ⚠ but it is the preferred instrument when the diagnosis needs a marker panel off the specimen, which is anaplastic carcinoma and lymphoma. Punch biopsy is for skin. Child, male, first-degree family history, and neck radiation are the clinical risk factors that raise the pre-test probability before any imaging.

lectures.name: Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Osteoporosis
lectures.title: Osteoporosis: Diagnosis, Risk and Treatment
lectures.framing: ⭐ You can diagnose osteoporosis three ways, and only one of them involves a bone density scan. A fragility fracture alone is enough, whatever the bone mineral density (BMD) says. That is the whole point of the treatment gap: a fracture is the diagnosis, and only 15% of patients are treated after a fragility fracture, against 80% who get a beta blocker after a heart attack. Once diagnosed, treatment choice turns on which fracture site you need to prevent and whether the patient has already failed or been harmed by an antiresorptive.
lectures.keypoints: A fragility fracture diagnoses osteoporosis on its own — but skull, hands, feet and ankles do not count, and neither does a genuinely traumatic fracture. T-score compares to a young adult, Z-score to age-matched peers; only the T-score diagnoses. raloxifene and teriparatide have no hip fracture data — reach for a bisphosphonate, denosumab, or estrogen when the hip is the concern. Every anabolic course must be followed by an antiresorptive, at 1 year for romosozumab and 2 for teriparatide. Osteonecrosis of the jaw has a definition with a clock in it: exposed bone unhealed at 8 weeks, and dental work goes first. Groin or thigh pain in a patient on a bisphosphonate is an impending atypical femoral fracture, not arthritis.

lectures.name: Overview of Metabolic Bone Disease
lectures.title: Metabolic Bone Disease: Osteomalacia, Paget's & Osteogenesis Imperfecta
lectures.framing: Three diseases of bone that are not osteoporosis, and ⭐ the lab panel separates all three before any imaging. Osteomalacia is a mineralization defect from vitamin D deficiency, so calcium and phosphate fall and alkaline phosphatase (ALP) rises. Paget's is disordered remodelling, so calcium and phosphate stay normal while ALP goes very high. Osteogenesis imperfecta is a collagen gene defect, so the panel is normal and the diagnosis is clinical. ⚠ Osteomalacia is routinely mistaken for osteoporosis, and the tell is that osteomalacia has overt symptoms while osteoporosis is indolent.
lectures.keypoints: ALP is the thread through all three: very high in Paget's, high in osteomalacia, normal in osteogenesis imperfecta. Calcium and phosphate are BOTH low in osteomalacia and BOTH normal in Paget's — that pair alone separates them. Urine calcium is LOW in osteomalacia, which is the opposite of what a stone-former's panel looks like. Proximal myopathy is the osteomalacia feature that osteoporosis never has, and it is what causes the falls. Bone-forming drugs are contraindicated in Paget's — you do not encourage a formation process that is already disordered, which makes zoledronate the answer and teriparatide the trap. Increased hat size and warmth over a bone are Paget's, and blue sclerae with fractures from birth are osteogenesis imperfecta. A young adult with celiac disease, falls, weakness and pseudofractures has osteomalacia, not osteoporosis.

Treat the bone disease when there are long bone deformities, vertebral compression fractures, or more than 3 fractures per year.

lectures.name: Embryology & Histology
lectures.title: Female Genital Histology & Early Embryogenesis
lectures.framing: Two halves that share one idea: ⭐ structure tells you what can go wrong there. In the histology half, the epithelium at each site predicts its disease — keratinized skin gets skin cancers, and the one place two epithelia meet is the one place cervical cancer starts. In the embryology half, the same teratogen does something completely different depending on the week it arrives, so timing, not the agent, is what the question is really testing.
lectures.keypoints: Keratin and adnexa separate labia majora from minora, and that is the whole histological question. The transformation zone is where two epithelia meet, which is why it is where cervical cancer arises and why the cancer can be of either type. Tubular glands mean proliferative and oestrogen; tortuous secretory glands mean luteal and progesterone. The functionalis sheds and the basalis rebuilds it. Fertilization happens in the ampulla, and the ampulla is also where an ectopic most often implants — same widest segment, same reason. The zona pellucida must degenerate before implantation can happen. Syncytiotrophoblast makes hCG; hCG maintains the corpus luteum until the placenta takes over at week 8. Every germ layer descends from the epiblast, and the hypoblast only ever makes the yolk sac lining. Weeks 3 to 8 is the critical period — before it, all or nothing; after it, minor anomalies only.

lectures.name: Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Gonadal Axis
lectures.title: The Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Gonadal Axis
lectures.framing: The axis is three tissues and one non-negotiable requirement: ⭐ gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) must arrive in PULSES. A continuous GnRH signal does not amplify the axis, it shuts it down, which is exactly how a GnRH agonist becomes a chemical castration. Everything else follows from two anatomical facts: the median eminence has no blood-brain barrier, so hypothalamic peptides can leave the brain, and parvicellular neurons feed the ANTERIOR pituitary through a portal system while magnocellular neurons bypass it into the POSTERIOR pituitary.
lectures.keypoints: Pulsatility is the whole axis. Continuous GnRH suppresses, which is why an agonist ends up doing the same job as an antagonist but with a dangerous surge first. kisspeptin is the strongest positive input to the pulse generator, and steroids never touch the GnRH neuron directly — they work through interneurons. LH → theca and Leydig; FSH → granulosa and Sertoli, and inhibin brakes FSH alone. The shared α subunit is why the β subunit is what gets measured. Cholesterol to pregnenolone, in the mitochondrion, is the rate-limiting step. Estradiol and progesterone act without further metabolism; testosterone usually does not. Estradiol induces the progesterone receptor, so the order of the cycle is built into the receptors themselves.

lectures.name: Approach to the Menstrual Cycle
lectures.title: The Menstrual Cycle
lectures.framing: One hormone does something no other hormone in the body does: ⭐ estradiol switches its own feedback from negative to positive. Below threshold it suppresses follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH); held above 300–500 pg/mL for about 48 hours it flips to feed-forward and triggers the luteinizing hormone (LH) surge. That single switch divides the cycle in two, and everything else is bookkeeping around it: the follicular phase is built by FSH and dismantled by the estradiol it produces; the luteal phase runs on progesterone and lasts a fixed two weeks unless an embryo arrives.
lectures.keypoints: Estradiol is the only hormone here that reverses the sign of its own feedback, and it needs both a level (300–500 pg/mL) and a duration (~48 hours) to do it. Getting one of those two right and the other wrong is the classic distractor. FSH falls during the follicular phase — counter-intuitively, because the follicle it grew is now making the oestrogen that suppresses it. The luteal phase is the fixed half of the cycle; when a cycle is short or long, it is the follicular phase that varies. The corpus luteum regresses after two weeks unless an embryo rescues it, and that regression is menstruation. Aromatization happens in the granulosa cell, on an androgen the theca cell made — remember which receptor sits on which cell and the rest follows.

The evidence that each piece is necessary, from the deck's two experiments:

Invariant is the point: the pituitary and ovary generate the cycle's shape, given only a steady pulse train.

- The ovary carries the cycle, not the brain's anatomy. Ovarian tissue transplanted subcutaneously to the abdomen of a castrated male rhesus monkey showed repetitive ovulatory cycles averaging 28 days.

lectures.name: Testicular and Ovarian Function
lectures.title: Testicular and Ovarian Function
lectures.framing: ⭐ The two gonads are the same machine with different settings. In both, luteinizing hormone (LH) acts on the steroid-making cell (Leydig, theca) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) acts on the nurse cell (Sertoli, granulosa), and in both the nurse cell makes inhibin to brake FSH. What differs is the output: spermatogenesis makes 4 haploid gametes continuously from a self-renewing stem cell; oogenesis makes 1 from a reservoir that was finished before birth. That single asymmetry explains menopause, polar bodies, and why the two arrest points exist at all.
lectures.keypoints: Map the four cells onto two hormones and you have the lecture: LH → Leydig and theca (androgen); FSH → Sertoli and granulosa (inhibin, and aromatase in the ovary). 4 gametes from spermatogenesis, 1 from oogenesis, and the female reservoir is fixed before birth. The oocyte is arrested twice: prophase I until recruitment, meiosis II until fertilization — fertilization is a trigger, not just a fusion. The blood-testis barrier exists because sperm are genetically foreign to their own host. Most FSH receptors wins the dominant-follicle competition, and assisted reproductive technology simply removes the competition by flooding the system. The granulosa cell trades FSH receptors for LH receptors as ovulation approaches — the same cell, answering to a different hormone. 5-α reductase makes DHT for hair, glands and external genitalia; aromatase makes estradiol and closes the growth plates. Only 5% of testosterone is free, and only that 5% works.

lectures.title: Physiologic Changes that Lead to Puberty
lectures.framing: Puberty is not switched on — the axis is built before birth, suppressed in infancy, and then DISINHIBITED. The menstrual cycle that follows runs on one hormone that reverses its own feedback.
lectures.keypoints: puberty is disinhibition, not activation. ⭐ The earliest measurable change is a NOCTURNAL rise in LH — before puberty LH is flat across 24 hours, and only in late puberty is it raised awake as well. Adrenarche is adrenal and separate from gonadarche, which is why pubic hair can appear with no gonadal activity. Most FSH receptors wins the dominant follicle. Ovulation is 36 hours after the surge. The follicular phase varies; the luteal phase does not. Boys end up taller because they start later, not because they grow faster.

  • Treatment — reassurance and explanation where timing is normal. ⚠ Irregular anovulatory cycles for >2 years after menarche are NORMAL and need no treatment. blocks.html: What lifts the brake — before puberty GABA inhibition dominates glutamate, so gonadotropin-releasing hormone output is low. Kisspeptin acting on GPR54 is the primary trigger, regulated by KNDy neurons (kisspeptin, neurokinin B, dynorphin), with leptin permissive and MKRN3 inhibitory. Proof: inactivating GPR54 mutations cause failure to progress through puberty and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, confirmed in knockout mice whose only major phenotype was reproductive.

The vocabulary is not interchangeable — gonadarche (gonads activated by LH/FSH) · adrenarche (adrenal androgens, a separate axis) · thelarche (breast, from ovarian estradiol) · pubarche (pubic hair, from adrenal androgen) · menarche · spermarche. Sequence in girls: adrenarche → gonadarche → thelarche → growth spurt → menarche, over 4-5 years.

Numbers — menarche mean 12.7 y; irregular anovulatory cycles are normal for >2 years afterwards. Cycle 21-35 days — only 15% of women have a 28-day cycle. Blood loss up to 80 mL. PMS affects 30-40%, PMDD 3-8%. Menopause = 12 months of amenorrhoea or FSH consistently >30, mean age 53. Genetics accounts for 50-75% of the variation in pubertal timing.

lectures.framing: Two numbers place every pubertal disorder: the age it happened, and the luteinizing hormone (LH). Age sets early against late; LH says whether the brain is driving it or something downstream is.

lectures.title: Anatomy of the Female Pelvis & Perineum
lectures.framing: Two lines organise the whole lecture: the pelvic pain line, which decides where pain is felt and which block reaches it, and the nodal watershed, which decides where a cancer spreads.
lectures.keypoints: ⭐ Above the pain line pain refers to flank and back along sympathetics; below it to buttock and thigh along parasympathetics — and that single line predicts both the presentation and the block. Ovarian artery from the aorta, uterine from the internal iliac, and their anastomosis is what lets the ovaries be spared at hysterectomy. Fundus drains para-aortic while cervix drains iliac — one organ, two basins. Clitoris drains to deep inguinal, labial skin to superficial.

• History — ⭐ WHERE is the pain referred? Flank, back and mid-trunk point above the pelvic pain line (fundus, tubes, ovaries); buttock, thigh and leg point below it (cervix, vagina). Then: cycle relationship, dyspareunia (superficial vs deep), bowel and bladder symptoms, obstetric and surgical history, trauma or straddle injury.
  • Physical exam — abdominal exam by quadrant · bimanual to size the uterus and assess mobility and adnexae · speculum for the cervix · through the thin vaginal wall you can palpate the cervix, ischial spines, sacral promontory, uterine artery pulsation and ovarian irregularity · perineum: perineal body integrity, scars, swelling and where it does and does not track.
  • Investigations — beta-human chorionic gonadotropin first in any woman of reproductive age · pelvic ultrasound (transvaginal) · hysterosalpingography (HSG) for tubal patency — contrast should spill into the peritoneum · culdocentesis via the posterior fornix for free fluid, since the rectouterine pouch is the lowest point when upright · staging imaging directed by the nodal basin: ⚠ fundus drains to para-aortic nodes, cervix to iliac, clitoris to DEEP inguinal, labial skin to SUPERFICIAL inguinal.

Surgery: at hysterectomy identify the ureter — water under the bridge — and the ovarian collateral lets the ovaries be spared.

lectures.name: Development of the Female Reproductive System
lectures.title: Development of the Female Reproductive System
lectures.framing: Female is the default: no testis-determining factor makes the ovary, no anti-Müllerian hormone keeps the Müllerian ducts, no testosterone dissolves the Wolffian ducts. Every anomaly below is one failed step in the fusion-and-canalisation sequence.
lectures.keypoints: Wolffian and Müllerian are reciprocal — one survives in each sex. Didelphys and bicornuate are failed FUSION; septate is failed RESORPTION; unicornuate is one duct that never formed. The vagina has two origins, upper third from the ducts and lower two-thirds from the bulbs. Absent vagina usually means absent uterus. ⭐ Always image the renal tract when a Müllerian anomaly is found — both systems arise from intermediate mesoderm, and urinary development precedes genital by about 10 days.

blocks.html: The sequence — primordial germ cells migrate from the yolk sac (weeks 4-6, ~T10) to the gonadal ridge; no migration, no gonad. Primitive sex cords degenerate, cortical cords form, oogonia become primary oocytes arrested in prophase I — ~400,000 at birth, and no oogonia form postnatally. Paramesonephric ducts open cranially as the tubes and fimbriae and fuse caudally into the uterovaginal primordium → uterus, cervix, upper 1/3 vagina; this induces the sinovaginal bulbs, which fuse into the vaginal plate and canalise into the lower 2/3. The hymen ruptures perinatally. Sexes are indifferent weeks 4-7 and distinct by week 12.

External genitalia — driven by estrogens and the absence of dihydrotestosterone, weeks 9-14: genital tubercle → clitoris, urethral folds → labia minora, labioscrotal swellings → labia majora. All three stay separated — female external development is defined by structures not fusing.

Descent — the gubernaculum tethers the ovary, which descends retroperitoneally but never enters the inguinal canal. Its midpoint splits into the ligament of the ovary and the round ligament of the uterus.

lectures.framing: Four words that are not synonyms — sex is biological, gender is psychological, gender identity is the person's own articulation, and sexual orientation is a separate axis entirely. The treatment ladder is then ordered by one thing: reversibility.
lectures.keypoints: dysphoria is the distress, not the incongruence. Blockers fully reversible, hormones partially, surgery not — and hormones wait until puberty has started. Fertility is discussed before hormones, not after. Comorbidity must be reasonably well-controlled, not cured.   • Investigations — before hormones: health history, risk assessment and relevant baseline labs; for testosterone, total testosterone plus sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) (⚠ SHBG falls in obesity and distorts the total; free androgen index = T/SHBG). ⚠ Oral testosterone cannot be monitored at all; injected testosterone is measured halfway between doses; transdermal any time.
  • Treatment — the ladder in reversibility order: puberty blockers (fully reversible) → gender-affirming hormones (partially reversible) → surgery (irreversible). ⚠ Hormones do not start until puberty has started. Criteria: persistent documented dysphoria · capacity to consent · age of majority or the adolescent SOC · ⚠ comorbidity "reasonably well-controlled", NOT resolved. Fertility preservation is discussed before hormones, not after.
  • Follow-up — ongoing monitoring of effectiveness and side effects, communication with primary care, mental health and surgeon. Surgery needs 1-2 mental health referrals; Ontario requires two providers.

blocks.html: Diagnosis — gender dysphoria is the DISTRESS, not the incongruence: marked and persistent incongruence, a desire to transition and be accepted as the experienced gender, a strong dislike of one's sexual anatomy or of anticipated pubertal changes. The assessment is summarised as insistence · persistence · consistence.

Epidemiology — 1 in 300 Canadians aged 15+, two-thirds under 35; 1.2-4.1% of adolescents. Prevalence is rising, not falling. Most PRE-pubertal children who identify as transgender do not persist; most ADOLESCENTS do — which is why puberty is where the ladder begins.

Outcomes — suicidality is 2-3× more frequent; 47% of trans youth in Ontario had considered suicide, 19% attempted. ⭐ Family support moves attempt risk from 60% to 4%, and youth managed with hormones, surgery where indicated and a multidisciplinary team including mental health clinicians had outcomes similar to the general population.

Guidelines — WPATH Standards of Care v8 (2022) and the Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline (2017). The endocrinologist's role is bounded: initial treatment considerations, advice when issues arise, and explicitly not necessarily diagnostic.

lectures.title: Disorders of Sexual Differentiation
lectures.framing: A disorder of sexual differentiation (DSD) is a discrepancy between karyotype, gonad, internal genitalia and external genitalia — so the karyotype is the first test, because it decides which half of the differential you are in.
lectures.keypoints: karyotype first. 5α-reductase deficiency virilises at puberty because testosterone is normal; androgen insensitivity cannot and feminises instead. T:DHT after hCG for the enzyme, DNA for the receptor. DHT builds the external genitalia, testosterone the internal ducts. ⭐ The 46,XX CAH infant looks ambiguous and is caught at birth; the 46,XY CAH infant looks normal and presents in salt-losing crisis at 1-3 weeks. Sex assignment does not inevitably mean surgery.

blocks.html: Workup skeleton

• History — family history of ambiguous genitalia, virilisation, infertility or unexplained neonatal death · pregnancy: maternal medications, maternal virilisation, maternal health · consanguinity · ⚠ neonatal crisis — vomiting, poor feeding, collapse at 1-3 weeks.
  • Physical exam — ⭐ PALPATE FOR GONADS — a palpable gonad is almost always a testis, which immediately narrows the differential · phallus length and width · labioscrotal folds: fused or open, rugated, hyperpigmented · number and position of urogenital openings · a drawn diagram, not prose · general exam for dysmorphism and for hyperpigmentation (ACTH excess).
  • Investigations — karyotype · pelvic and abdominal ultrasound · 17-hydroxyprogesterone (markedly raised in 21-hydroxylase deficiency) · electrolytes and glucose — Na↓, K↑, acidosis, hypoglycaemia · then directed: T:DHT ratio after hCG stimulation for 5α-reductase deficiency, DNA analysis for androgen insensitivity.
  • Treatment — CAH: lifelong hydrocortisone 10-15 mg/m²/day divided, plus fludrocortisone 0.05-0.20 mg, with extra oral saline in infants and ⚠ stress dosing during illness to prevent a salt-losing crisis. ⚠ Sex assignment does not inevitably mean surgery — evidence for the operations is lacking and only expert surgeons should be involved.
  • Follow-up — ⚠ delay assignment of sex of rearing until investigations are complete; do not assign a name; do not register the birth · neutral terms throughout: gonads, phallus, labioscrotal folds · warn that a final diagnosis may take several weeks · multidisciplinary team with psychology and social work.

blocks.html: Salt wasting vs simple virilising vs non-classic — set by residual enzyme activity: <1% = salt wasting (75% of 21-hydroxylase deficiency), crisis at 1-3 weeks, fatal if missed · 1-5% = simple virilising, cortisol deficiency and androgen excess without significant salt loss · mild mutation = non-classic, presenting as premature pubarche then a polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome-like picture.

Assessing a newborn — palpate for gonads (a palpable gonad is almost always a testis) · describe and diagram the labioscrotal folds, phallus, and number/position of urogenital openings · karyotype, pelvic ultrasound, 17-hydroxyprogesterone. Use neutral terms: gonads, phallus, labio-scrotal folds. Delay assignment of sex of rearing, do not assign a name, do not register the birth. Refer to a tertiary centre — endocrinology, neonatology, genetics, gynaecology, urology, social work.

lectures.name: Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS)
lectures.title: Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS)
lectures.framing: Renamed from polycystic ovary syndrome in 2026 because both halves of the old name were wrong. The diagnosis is a triad that needs no ultrasound, and it is made by excluding the mimics of each limb separately — hyperandrogenism has its own list of them, ovulatory dysfunction has another.
lectures.keypoints: the follicles are arrested antral follicles and the ovary is a target, not the source — which is why the name changed. ⭐ Hyperandrogenism plus oligomenorrhoea plus clean exclusions is diagnostic without ever scanning her; ultrasound is an alternative route into the second limb, not a criterion of its own. ⚠ Cystic ovaries are also not specific — they occur early after menarche and in normally cycling women, so the scan is neither required for the diagnosis nor sufficient for it. ⭐ Testosterone only reads against its two ranges — female normal < 2 nmol/L, male from ~8 — so 2.1-2.5 is fractionally over and fits, while 10 is a male level and means a tumour; ⚠ and a normal testosterone does not exclude PMOS, because clinical hyperandrogenism satisfies that limb by itself. 17-hydroxyprogesterone is what separates non-classic CAH from PMOS when the picture is otherwise identical. Acanthosis is the insulin sign; striae would mean Cushing's. ⚠ Hirsutism is defined by distress, not by a score — the modified Ferriman-Gallwey grades it but ignores ethnicity and hair removal. Of the five treatments offered, only topical testosterone is wrong. Reassure that she can conceive — and advise contraception in the same breath.

blocks.html: Workup skeleton

• History (hirsutism) — location, timing of onset and rate of onset · location and timing of acne · presence and timing of alopecia · family history of hirsutism · ⚠ rate of onset, ethnicity and parental appearance must all be weighed before calling hair growth abnormal · ⚠ a rapid onset is the tumour question, not a PMOS one.
  • History (oligomenorrhoea) — age at menarche and how often periods came initially, in the later teens, and after age 20 · oral contraceptive use · ⚠ galactorrhoea, whose absence is what removes the prolactinoma · family history of irregular menses and infertility · a gentle weight history — did the cycle become irregular after significant weight gain · personal history of prediabetes, obstructive sleep apnoea or metabolic liver disease · fertility intentions and current contraception · family history of gestational diabetes and type 2 diabetes · mood · medications. ⚠ If menses became irregular on stopping an oral contraceptive pill, the oral contraceptive pill did not cause it — it masked oligomenorrhoea she already had.
  • Physical exam — blood pressure, BMI, and central adipose distribution — visual assessment can suffice, or waist ÷ hip, over 0.85 in women · ⭐ acanthosis nigricans over the back of the neck and in the axilla, with skin tags beside it — the insulin-resistance signs · terminal hair in a male pattern (face, chin, chest, upper arms), acne, frontal alopecia · score the hair with the modified Ferriman-Gallwey system — 9 sites, each graded 1-4 · ⚠ striae are NOT expected — violaceous striae point at Cushing's instead.
  • Investigations — the exclusion panel first: beta-hCG · prolactin (normal < 20 nmol/L) · TSH, with free T4 if it is suppressed · total testosterone. ⚠ Read testosterone against both ranges: normal female is < 2 nmol/L, the male range starts ~8. A level of 2.1-2.5 nmol/L is fractionally over the female ceiling and fits PMOS; 10 nmol/L is inside the male range and suggests an androgen-secreting tumour. ⚠ A normal testosterone does not exclude PMOS — clinical hyperandrogenism satisfies the limb on its own. 17-hydroxyprogesterone where non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) is in question. Then metabolic screening: fasting glucose or A1c, lipid panel. ⚠ Pelvic ultrasound is NOT required — hyperandrogenism plus oligomenorrhoea plus clean exclusions is already diagnostic.
  • Treatment — treat the symptom of distress: BCP or cyclical progesterone for oligomenorrhoea · aromatase inhibitors to induce ovulation, metformin arguably for early miscarriage · antiandrogens and eflornithine for hirsutism · minoxidil 5% for alopecia. Lifestyle throughout: high fibre, low fat, ~30 min planned exercise daily, modest weight loss — ⚠ "no body shaming". Only topical testosterone is the wrong answer.
  • Follow-up — ⚠ induce withdrawal bleeds at least 4× a year and image for endometrial hypertrophy (carcinoma risk) · monitor for DM, HTN and cardiovascular disease, 150 min vigorous exercise weekly · counsel that she can conceive spontaneously, so contraception is still needed.

blocks.html: The lecture's own exclusion list is seven — pregnancy · hyperprolactinaemia · exogenous testosterone · tumour producing testosterone · CAH · hyperthyroidism · early menarche or menopause. Cushing syndrome keeps a column here but is not on that list: the deck names adrenal Cushing's only as a source of an androgen-secreting tumour, while the lecture's case still argues against Cushing's explicitly, on absent striae and a normal fasting glucose.

Three of the seven have no column, because the history rather than a disease process is what finds them — exogenous androgen (taking testosterone, or skin contact with a partner's topical testosterone, found only on a thorough medication and social history) · pregnancy (suspected on history, settled by beta-hCG) · early menarche or menopause (a thorough menstrual history, and no test beyond it). Rate of onset is the other history discriminator: PMOS hirsutism creeps over years, a tumour's arrives fast.

Managing risk — metabolic: monitor for DM, HTN and cardiovascular disease · 150 minutes planned vigorous exercise weekly, high-fibre low-fat diet, modest weight loss · consider bariatric surgery, "quite effective for restoring menstrual cycles and fertility". Endometrial carcinoma: induce withdrawal bleeds at least 4× a year with an oral contraceptive or cyclical progesterone, plus ultrasound surveillance for hypertrophy.
Also more common in PMOS — endometrial carcinoma · gestational diabetes · central adipose distribution · frontal alopecia. Adrenal hypertrophy is not.

Myths the module asks you to dispel — TRUE: subfertility and early miscarriage · metabolic syndrome correlates · endometrial cancer · mood disorders. FALSE: cannot lose weight · constantly hungry · organic or vegan diet helps · cannot conceive. Every false one blames the patient; every true one is a real clinical risk. Counsel with "no body shaming" and meet patients where they are.
